title: Convoy No. 91, 3–4 July 1944
eyebrow: Marianas lifeguard and Luzon Strait · BANG's second war patrol, in a pack with SEAHORSE and GROWLER

paras.text: SEAHORSE's and BANG's attacks on convoy No. 91 southwest of Pratas Island, as typed on their attack sheets, beside the Hong Kong fleet's table of the destroyer Kuri's reports.

The Japanese record is the 2nd China Expeditionary Fleet's (Hong Kong) table of submarine reports for July 1944 (jacar:C08030032900 p28), from the destroyer Kuri (栗). SEAHORSE attacked first, at 2354–2355 H on 3 July (0054–0055 I), and claimed two freighters sunk; Kuri reported Nitto Maru torpedoed and sunk at 0100 I, 19-21N 115-50E. BANG fired at 0506 I on what was left of the convoy; Kuri reported being under torpedo attack with no damage at 0515 I, and SEAHORSE logged depth charges eleven minutes after BANG fired "(Bang?)". SEAHORSE attacked again at 1238–1239 H and claimed two passenger freighters; Kuri reported Gyoyu Maru and No. 28 Kyodo Maru torpedoed and sunk at 1345 I, 20-18N 115-02E. The diary's narrative (p27) names it 第九一船団 (No. 91 convoy), attacked southwest of Pratas Island by two or three submarines; its ports are not recorded there, and its course (270, then 320–335 on SEAHORSE's sheets) points to Hong Kong. FRUPAC's "torp attack 0105/04" fits SEAHORSE's first attack.

Takao to Hong Kong (secondary, industrialhistoryhk:29957); SEAHORSE's course fits. SEAHORSE saw five freighters with two destroyers and other escorts; BANG saw one AK. The convoy's own record: [[convoy:no-91-1944-07]].

Positions are BANG's own dead reckoning and star sights; lines between them are straight, and where she went in between is not recorded. Open circles are ships she sighted, at the target's position. As the clock passes each firing time a red ring pulses at BANG's position; hover a diamond for the attack sheet.

BANG kept zone K (−10) for Attack 1 and zone I (−9) for Attacks 2 and 3, as her report does; GROWLER kept I on station, but SEAHORSE kept H (−8). Japanese records use Tokyo time (I, −9): the escort division's chart has HI-67's two oilers hit at 1515, seven minutes after BANG's sheet.

No Japanese record has been found yet for Attacks 1 and 3; those actions show only the American side. Where the Japanese record names only the ships that were hit, the rest of the convoy is described as the boats saw it.

BANG's second war patrol report, NARA microfilm M1752 (74802784); SEAHORSE Patrol 5 (74845019); GROWLER Patrol 9 (74818866). The 1st Surface Escort Division war diary, June 1944, via JACAR (C08030141000, National Institute for Defense Studies). Sarawak Maru's record from combinedfleet.com, a secondary source, flagged where used. Coastline: Natural Earth.

Also read Agekumo Maru; ex Ethel Moller, 912 GRT (the comment). The post summarises a BAAG report: arrived Hong Kong from Shanghai via Formosa, inward cargo anti-aircraft guns and ammunition, discharged 21-22 July to the Tsim Sha Tsui barracks; it dates the arrival 20 July. A reader's comment (P. Cundall, 4 Dec 2018, no source cited) puts her in TA-406 Shanghai to Takao and then No. 91 Takao to Hong Kong with Nitto, Kyodo No. 28 and Gyoyu Maru, the only one of four to survive, arriving 5 July. Not yet in a Japanese record

paras.text: Attacked southwest of Pratas Island (東沙島) on 4 July 1944; the diary estimated two or three submarines. SEAHORSE's attacks pair with Kuri's two sinking reports by time and place; BANG's with Kuri's 0515 "no damage" report by time alone (inferred). **Ports, cargo and the number of ships are not recorded** in the 2nd China Expeditionary Fleet diary. "To Hong Kong" is inferred from the course on SEAHORSE's attack sheets (270, then 320–335) and the escorts, which were Hong Kong's (Kuri and Hatsukari escort another convoy off 碣石湾 on 29 July, p26). SEAHORSE counted five freighters and two destroyers with other escorts.

A secondary account fills in the route: a reader's comment on the Industrial History of Hong Kong post about Gyoun Maru (industrialhistoryhk:29957, no source cited) says four ships came from Shanghai to Takao as TA-406 and went on to Hong Kong as No. 91, and that Gyoun Maru alone survived, reaching Hong Kong on 5 July. The post's BAAG summary has her inward cargo as anti-aircraft guns and ammunition (but an arrival date of 20 July). Four ships agrees with three sunk and one surviving; SEAHORSE counted five freighters.
To find: a Japanese record of the sailing port (Takao, Manila or Yulin), and whether Nitto, Gyoyu or No. 28 Kyodo Maru has a movement log with her cargo.
